summaries.summary: Semantic Role Labeling (SRL) is important in Natural Language Processing (NLP) for information extraction, question answering, and other NLP tasks, finding predicate-argument structure.
INLINEFORM0 is shown.
The predicate WRITE has arguments `Mike' as A0 or writer and `a book' as A1 or thing written, with A0 and A1 corresponding to PropBank annotations BIBREF0.
Insufficient manually annotated corpora motivate unsupervised SRL BIBREF1, BIBREF2, BIBREF3, which may benefit from word alignment information in parallel text BIBREF4, BIBREF5, BIBREF6.
With alignments Mike-Mike, written-geschrieben, and book-Buch, the system might predict A1 for Buch, making SRL systems more accurate using parallel data.
The paper proposes a joint Bayesian model for unsupervised semantic role induction in multiple languages, with individual Bayesian models and crosslingual latent variables for soft role agreement.
The paper begins by describing the unsupervised SRL pipeline and monolingual semantic role induction model, then describes the multilingual model.
Following previous work BIBREF7, BIBREF8, the authors use a standard unsupervised SRL setup consisting of the following steps.
The modeled task, unsupervised semantic role induction, is step 4 of this pipeline.
The base monolingual model is the Bayesian model of garg2012unsupervised, with predicate-specific semantic roles and role inventories divided into Primary and Secondary roles.
A complete role sequence defines ordering as the sequence of PRs, intervals between consecutive PRs, SRs, empty intervals, and evaluation mappings to gold roles.
Figure FIGREF16 illustrates two copies of the monolingual model on either side of the crosslingual latent variables, followed by the generative process.
All multinomial and binomial distributions have symmetric Dirichlet and beta priors respectively, and Figure FIGREF7 gives probability equations for the monolingual model.
The multilingual model uses word alignments in a parallel corpus, copies the monolingual model for each language, and adds crosslingual latent variables (CLVs) coupling aligned roles.
Every predicate-tuple has its own CLVs, each a multi-valued variable defining peaky distributions over role labels for each language, generated via a Chinese Restaurant Process BIBREF11.
The multilingual model is deficient because aligned roles are generated twice, so an approximation treats each aligned role as generated by the monolingual model and corresponding CLV.
This is the first work to incorporate coupling of aligned arguments directly in a Bayesian SRL model, and it scales gracefully to more than two languages.
One joint Bayesian model supports semi-supervised learning settings by fixing annotated variables during training, including labeled source data and no labeled target data.
Inference predicts role labels and CLVs from predicate, voice, and syntactic features using collapsed Gibbs-sampling, then calculates the MAP estimate of model parameters.

DISPLAYFORM0 is shown.
The integral has a closed form solution due to Dirichlet-multinomial conjugacy, with subscripts INLINEFORM0, INLINEFORM1, INLINEFORM2, and INLINEFORM3 defined.
Sampling roles in the multilingual model also requires considering probabilities of roles being generated by the CLVs.
Sampling CLVs requires three factors: two probabilities of generating aligned roles and one selecting the CLV according to CRP.
Aligned roles INLINEFORM0 and INLINEFORM1 are connected to INLINEFORM2, and INLINEFORM3 refers to all variables except INLINEFORM4, INLINEFORM5, and INLINEFORM6.
Trained parameters parse monolingual data using the monolingual model, ignoring crosslingual parameters, so CLVs act as a regularizer for monolingual models.
Evaluation uses correctly identified arguments and the lang2011unsupervised metric with Purity (PU), Collocation (CO), and F1, weighted by argument instances.
The baseline from lang2011unsupervised assigns semantic roles based on syntactic function, giving clusters to INLINEFORM1 most frequent syntactic functions and the rest to the INLINEFORM2 th cluster.

This work relates to titovcrosslingual, whose separate monolingual models use an extra penalty term, inefficient optimization, annotation-projection-like inference, and no natural scaling beyond two languages.
The monolingual model BIBREF3 has global role ordering probability and avoids hard clustering by argument-keys, unlike titovcrosslingual.

Experiments use English (EN) and German (DE) CoNLL 2009 and EN-DE Europarl, with about 40k EN and 36k DE CoNLL sentences, about 1.5M parallel EN-DE sentences, 3.4M EN predicate instances, 2.62M DE predicate instances, 9.3M EN arguments, 4.43M DE arguments, and 0.76M aligned arguments.
Since CoNLL annotations have 21 semantic roles, the model and baseline use 21 roles, with PRs set to 2 and SRs to 21-2=19.
In the first setting (Line 1), monolingual training and testing on CoNLL data significantly improves F1 over Baseline (Line 0) in both languages.
In the second setting (Line 2), additional monolingual Europarl (EP) data gives equivalent English results and significant German improvement compared with Line 1.
The third setting (Line 3) adds word alignments in EP data, yielding non-significant improvements in both languages compared with Line 2.
Training only on EP and testing on CoNLL, Lines 4 and 5 show small multilingual model improvements in both languages.
Little information can be learned about semantic roles from this parallel data setup, with only 8% of English arguments and 17% of German arguments aligned.
In an annotation transfer scenario with small labeled source data and large parallel unlabeled data, clamping source CoNLL role annotations yields small improvements in target languages.
The semi-supervised monolingual setting randomly selects INLINEFORM0 CoNLL sentences as supervised and keeps the rest INLINEFORM1 unsupervised, clamping supervised role labels.
A supervised baseline calculates a MAP estimate for predicates seen in supervised sentences and uses the standard baseline for unseen predicates.
Figures FIGREF33 and FIGREF33 show performance variation with INLINEFORM0, followed by observations.
[leftmargin=*] is shown.
At around INLINEFORM0, the supervised baseline starts outperforming the semi-supervised model, with 10% labeling about 3.6k German sentences and 4k English sentences.
For German, about 3.5% or 1260 supervised sentences match the increase from 1.5M unlabeled sentences, and about 180 more cover the alignments benefit.
On a completely unseen CoNLL test set, clustering evaluation is less reliable, but the same pattern was broadly obtained.
This work relates to titovcrosslingual, uses superlingual latent variables from naseem2009multilingual, and discusses pado2009cross and furstenau2009graph transfer and alignment approaches.

Monolingual unsupervised SRL work includes swier2004unsupervised on the British National Corpus with 54 verbs from VerbNet, Bayesian models by garg2012unsupervised and titov2012bayesian, and other approaches.

The proposed Bayesian SRI model uses crosslingual latent variables, is evaluated in four training scenarios, and finds limited parallel-corpus gains but strong benefits from annotating small amounts of data.
Future work includes training on different language pairs, on more than two languages, and with more inclusive models of role alignment.
This work was funded by the Swiss NSF grant 200021_125137 and EC FP7 grant PARLANCE.
